open_obligations: Check whether Parrish et al.'s snippet (PS) baseline is the right analogue of Khan et al.'s naive baseline.
Note the difference between human-written single-turn arguments and multi-round LLM debate.
Check judge selection: 21 filtered judges versus 194 MTurk workers.
in.other_title: Human judges 88% with debate vs 78% consultancy; LLM judges 76% vs 54% (naive 60% / 48%)
in.rationale: Parrish et al. report human-written single-turn arguments did not improve time-limited judges' accuracy. Khan et al. report non-expert human judges reach 88% with 3-round LLM debate versus 60% naive on QuALITY HARD; Khan et al.'s judges cannot read the story and see verified quotes, while Parrish et al.'s have 90 s of passage access and snippets, so the null and positive results come from different information conditions.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether debate-style arguments improve accuracy of non-expert judges on hard QuALITY questions

open_obligations: Check that both studies use comparable hard QuALITY subsets, given the two-turn study reuses the single-turn arguments
Note that judges differ (Upwork judges with a 5-minute limit here vs MTurk judges with 90 seconds of passage access in the single-turn study)
Confirm the baselines match: the two-turn study compares PSA with PS only, without the passage-only condition
in.other_title: Two-turn counter-arguments also fail to help, mirroring Parrish et al.'s single-turn null result
in.rationale: The authors explicitly describe their two-turn null result as mirroring Parrish et al.'s single-turn null result in a closely matched setting (same arguments, passages and questions), so the findings agree.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether debate-style arguments help human judges on hard reading comprehension; holds for one or two turns of human-written arguments with snippets available in both conditions

open_obligations: Read p14 L47-51, where the authors say their absolute accuracies are not comparable to Parrish et al.'s
Note that Parrish et al.'s judges had 90 seconds of passage access, while Michael et al.'s judges never see the passage
Compare question sampling: Michael et al. keep only Gutenberg QuALITY-hard questions needing more than one or two sentences of context
in.other_title: Michael et al. find debate helps QuALITY judges, unlike Parrish et al.'s single-turn null result
in.rationale: Both studies ask whether debate helps human judges on QuALITY reading comprehension; Parrish et al. report a null result, while Michael et al. find debate beats consultancy (84% vs 74%). The authors say absolute accuracies are not comparable (p14 L47-48) and attribute the difference to protocol, so this challenges how far the null result generalizes, not its internal validity.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether debate improves human judge accuracy on hard QuALITY questions; the contrast depends on protocol differences (length, judge interaction, expertise gap)

text: The authors report that human-written single arguments for a correct and an incorrect answer option, shown side by side, did not improve the accuracy of time-limited human judges who had not read the full passage on long-context multiple-choice questions. A baseline condition that showed only human-selected text snippets (no arguments) did improve accuracy.
title: Single-turn debate-style arguments do not improve human accuracy on hard QuALITY questions
